content: 1. The responsible and prudent use of anthelmintic chemicals is essential to control anthelmintic resistance in grazing livestock species. It is recommended to always use registered products of adequate quality, whether they are well-known brands or generic products. 2. Pharmacovigilance is critical and should be included in national regulations. Competent authorities responsible for veterinary drug registration must establish and implement an efficient regulatory framework for the registration of antiparasitics and monitor their safe and effective use once they are available on the market. 3. Dialogue between regulatory authorities and pharmaceutical companies should be promoted to emphasize the importance of the problem and ensure that both parties fulfill their roles in using quality products and implementing measures to reduce parasite resistance. 4. An American network of regulatory agencies that cooperates and exchanges information about antiparasitic products and resistance would be beneficial. 5. In some countries, information brochures have been developed for producers, explaining the available medications for fasciolosis, the appropriate doses for approved species, and the withdrawal periods. These materials are useful for informing veterinary professionals and local producers and are a recommended practice. 6. Treatment strategies for animal fasciolosis can be curative or strategic and preventive. Strategic and preventive treatment is preferred, focusing on reducing parasite numbers in hosts and pastures with minimal treatments per year to lower the risk of resistance, disease prevalence, and economic losses. 7. Curative treatment is necessary when clinical symptoms are present. In acute cases, medications effective against immature parasite stages should be used. 8. Strategic treatment should be based on local epidemiology to determine the optimal timing for maximum effect with minimal treatments. This depends on regional climate characteristics, transmission patterns, and other factors such as animal management, available medications, and socioeconomic conditions of producers. 9. Each region should develop its own treatment schedule for fasciolosis based on local epidemiology, species present, available medications, and producers’ socioeconomic conditions. Relevant authorities, producer associations, and veterinary professionals should collaborate to create and promote these schedules. 10. Pasture management and other strategies, such as fencing high-risk areas, avoiding co-grazing of susceptible species, rotational grazing, and using good-quality hay or silage, are essential to reduce and prevent transmission. 11. In family farming systems, implementing these measures may be challenging due to cost or feasibility. Veterinary professionals and outreach personnel should work with family farmers to identify the most serious problems, reduce risk areas, and implement appropriate management measures. 12. Animal movement can spread fasciolosis by contaminating water sources and pastures. Proper animal treatment, quarantines, and pasture management can minimize this risk. 13. Policies from the Ministry of Agriculture (or equivalent) should support subnational levels in implementing fasciolosis control measures, especially for small family farmers. This includes providing a legislative framework for registering quality anti-fasciolosis products, conducting pharmacovigilance, and supporting field implementation. 14. Technical support should include developing and promoting region-appropriate fasciolosis control strategies, demonstrating economic benefits, and providing resources such as medicines and logistics to family farmers in affected areas. 15. People acquire fasciolosis by ingesting metacercariae present in contaminated food and water. Sources of infection include aquatic plants, irrigated terrestrial plants, contaminated water, and improperly handled vegetables. 16. Food safety measures include avoiding consumption of aquatic plants from risk areas, using uncontaminated water for irrigation and washing, and cooking vegetables at 60°C. Chemical treatments and refrigeration are not effective control methods. 17. Water safety measures include using safe water, avoiding water from areas with snail hosts, boiling or filtering suspicious water, and ensuring filters can block metacercariae. Chlorination alone is insufficient. 18. Livers infected with fasciolosis should be discarded as they are unsuitable for human consumption.
